source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:35 (the Ramah: 'this alone lacks the yod; every slaves-word in the Torah plene')
claim_en: THE ONE LEAN SLAVES-WORD: ועבדם ('flocks and herds, silver and gold, AND SLAVES...' — the servant reciting Abraham's wealth, 24:35) — UNIQUE in the Torah and written DEFECTIVE (no yod), while every other slaves-word runs plene (builder-asserted over the whole plene family): the inventory-boast goes lean exactly at the human line.
middah: ink (the written form — the Masorah's note)

source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:39 ('אלי written defective — and our rabbis expounded it in Bereshit Rabbah 59: Eliezer had a daughter and sought to give her to Isaac'; Rashi cited; Yalkut Hosea 528; the Gur Aryeh's resolution)
claim_en: THE SERVANT'S SECRET HOPE: אלי ('PERHAPS the woman will not follow me' — the oath retold, 24:39) — written DEFECTIVE, no vav: the perhaps-word collapses into TO-ME, and the midrash reads Eliezer's daughter-wish in the dropped letter ('Canaan holds deceitful scales,' Hos 12:8 behind it). SNAPSHOT: the qubutz-pointed lean perhaps is UNIQUE in the whole DB (builder-asserted single token)...
middah: ink (the written form — the Masorah's note)

source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:39 (the plene control at the first telling)
claim_en: ...while at the FIRST telling, face to face with Abraham, the same servant's perhaps is written FULL (אולי, 24:5): the hope hides only in the retelling — the letter drops the vav exactly where the midrash drops the mask.
middah: ink (the written form — the Masorah's note)

source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:27 ('the second — with chirik'; pair completion from the road-thanksgiving)
claim_en: ONE VOWEL NARROWS THE FAMILY, completed: at the retelling's thanksgiving the same consonants take CHIRIK — בת אחי אדני ('the daughter of my master's BROTHER,' singular, 24:48) against the tzere plural of 24:27: the road-prayer thanked the whole kin-house; the report names one man.
middah: ink (the written form — the Masorah's note)

claim_en: ומגדנת ('and PRECIOUS THINGS to her brother and mother') — UNIQUE in the Torah, and the dalet carries dagesh as ruled: the gift-word appears once, dotted, at the bride-price.

source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:53 (the dagesh leg)

source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:55 ('one of the verses our rabbis called ITUR SOFERIM — the scribes' adornment — as I wrote at the end of Behaalotekha')
claim_en: THE SCRIBES' ADORNMENT, SECOND TORAH MEMBER: אחר תלך ('let the maiden stay... AFTERWARD she shall go,' 24:55) — written bare אחר with no joining vav, one of the itur soferim (the scribes' adornment-list of expected-but-omitted vavs); the corpus's first member stands at frozen 18:5 ('AFTERWARD you shall pass on'). SNAPSHOT: bare, as the list requires.
middah: ink (the written form — the Masorah's note)

source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:60 ('ויברכו — the resh with SHEVA')
claim_en: DISCREPANCY, THIRD STATION: ויברכו ('and they BLESSED Rebecca') — Minchat Shai rules the resh with plain sheva; SNAPSHOT points HATAF PATACH (the compound half-vowel): the bless-word vocalization split now counts three stations in the codex line (12:3's career-law, 22:18's Aqedah blessing, and the bride's send-off). Watchlist.
middah: ink (the written form — the Masorah's note)

source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:60 ('the Hilleli copy: וירש; the Jerusalem: ויירש with the Masorah-note UNIQUE-PLENE — and so the precise books and the Ramah: plene')
claim_en: ויירש ('may your seed INHERIT the gate of its haters') — SNAPSHOT writes it PLENE, both yods, with the Jerusalem copy, the precise books and the Ramah's whole-Torah rule (frozen G38-07/08/09: the one defective inherit-verb is the Aqedah's), against the Hilleli's lean reading — the manuscript split named, the codex side declared.

source: Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Gen 24:60 (רבבה four in the Masorah; the two-chase-a-myriad and the myriad-of-the-field named to her)
claim_en: רבבה ('be thou mother to thousands of MYRIADS') — THREE tokens in the Torah: Rebecca's blessing (24:60), the two-chase-a-myriad (Lev 26:8), the how-should-one-chase-a-myriad (Deut 32:30); the Masorah's fourth is Ezekiel's myriad-as-the-field-growth (Ezek 16:7; edge) — the bride blessed into the war-arithmetic of her children.
middah: E7 (the concordance pair — the same wording at two seats, the Kitzur's reading at narrative strength)

source: Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Gen 24:67 ('ויבאה — two in the Masorah, in the book of Genesis, written defective; its letters count TWENTY-FOUR — she was adorned with twenty-four adornments')
claim_en: THE TWO BROUGHT BRIDES: ויבאה ('and he BROUGHT HER into the tent of Sarah his mother') — exactly TWICE in the Torah, both in Genesis: God bringing the first woman to the first man ('and He BROUGHT HER to the man,' 2:22) and Isaac bringing Rebecca into his mother's tent (24:67) — the Torah's only two bride-deliveries, one written form. And the lean word's letters count 6+10+2+1+5 = TWENTY-FOUR: the Kitzur's twenty-four adornments riding the sum.
middah: E7 (the concordance pair — the two brought brides; the letter-count of twenty-four, E29, rides beside)

source: Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Gen 24:67 (האהלה eight in the Masorah — the eight dwellings of the Presence)
claim_en: האהלה ('INTO THE TENT') — SIX tokens in the Torah: Sarah's tent at the annunciation (18:6), Rebecca's entry (24:67), Jethro's welcome (Exod 18:7), the tent of meeting twice (Exod 33:8-9), Eldad and Medad's hour (Num 11:26); the Kitzur's eight-list spans Tanakh toward the Presence's eight dwellings (edges) — the tent-word with the leading-heh gathers the Shekhinah-stations.
middah: E7 (the concordance pair — the same wording at two seats, the Kitzur's reading at narrative strength)

source: Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Gen 24:67 ('ויאהבה — two in the Masorah: here and Amnon's; there love hung on a thing and lapsed; here it hung on nothing and stood')
claim_en: ויאהבה ('and he LOVED HER') — UNIQUE in the Torah: Isaac's love appears once in the letter; the Masorah's pair-leg is Amnon's collapsing love (II Sam 13:1; edge) — love hung on a thing lapses, Isaac's stood.
middah: E7 (the concordance pair — the same wording at two seats, the Kitzur's reading at narrative strength)

source: Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Gen 24:7 ('מלאכו written TWICE — he asked for one angel on the going and one on the return')
claim_en: מלאכו ('He shall send HIS ANGEL before you') — exactly TWO tokens in the Torah, BOTH in this chapter: Abraham's promise for the going (24:7) and the servant's retelling for the return (24:40) — one angel out, one angel back, precisely the Kitzur's count.
middah: E7 (the concordance pair — the same wording at two seats, the Kitzur's reading at narrative strength)

source: Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Gen 24:56 ('אל תאחרו אתי וה׳ — the final letters: ESCORT — for they escorted him')
claim_en: THE ESCORT IN THE FINALS: אל תאחרו אתי ויהוה ('do not DELAY me, since YHWH has prospered my way,' 24:56) — the four words close ל-ו-י-ה: the letters of לויה ('escort'), in order — the send-off written into the seams of the impatience-verse.
middah: E30 (notarikon — the initials, finals, or rearranged letters of the verse's own words, the Kitzur's reading)

source: Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Gen 24:58 ('עם האיש הזה — the final letters: MOSES — she went according to the law of Moses and Israel')
claim_en: MOSES IN THE CONSENT: התלכי עם האיש הזה ('will you GO with this man?') — the three question-closing words end ם-ש-ה: the letters of משה ('Moses'), in order — the Kitzur reads the bride's free consent as already under the law of Moses and Israel.
middah: E30 (notarikon — the initials, finals, or rearranged letters of the verse's own words, the Kitzur's reading)

source: Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Gen 24:47 ('ואשם — lacking the yod: he did not touch her flesh, not even with the yod of his fingers, out of modesty')
claim_en: ואשם ('and I PLACED the ring on her nose' — the retelling, 24:47) — written WITHOUT the yod (builder-asserted), and the Kitzur rides the missing letter: he placed without touching, 'not even with the yod of his fingers.'
middah: ink (the verse's own count or written form — the Kitzur's homily on it, no rule moved)

claim_en: THE OATH NARROWS IN THE RETELLING: Abraham swears the servant against the Canaanites אשר אנכי יושב בקרבו ('in whose MIDST I dwell,' 24:3)...

claim_en: הלזה ('who is THIS MAN walking in the field toward us?') — heh in patach as ruled, and the word stands exactly TWICE in the Torah: Rebecca's first sight of Isaac (24:65) and the brothers' 'behold, THIS dreamer comes' (37:19) — the this-one word opens on a bridegroom and returns on a betrayal.

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:10
claim_en: THE MATCH IS TRACED TO THE PREVIOUS BLOCK'S ALTAR, AND THE TRACE IS DISPUTED. 'The matter came forth from the LORD' is read as coming from Mount Moriah - the match decreed at the binding, so that Laban's own mouth witnesses a thread the machine records in gen_38. The Rabbis dissent and answer from the verse's own tail instead. Both are kept; the chain does not settle where the decree was issued.

check.note: A cross-block causal claim placed in an antagonist's mouth, with the dissent preserved.

middah: plain (a teacher's statement — an identification, a narrative expansion, a recorded dispute, or the verse's own wording read as the rule; no catalogued inference form)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:12; Mishnah Ketubot 5:2
claim_en: A MISSING CHARACTER IS ACCOUNTED FOR, AND THE DELAY IS RE-READ AS HIS FUNERAL. The father speaks at 24:50 and is gone by 24:55; the chain answers that he sought to impede and was struck down overnight, proved from the double reading of a verse about the upright and the wicked. The delay the family then asks for is re-read accordingly - 'days' as the seven days of mourning, for him - and the alternative 'or ten' as the twelve-month preparation a virgin is allowed, the received bride-time ruling seated on this verse.

check.note: A narrative gap filled by a death, with the following request re-read as mourning and a case-shelf allowance seated on it.

middah: plain (the missing father accounted for; days and or-ten read as durations)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:12; Onkelos Genesis 24:57
claim_en: A MARRIAGE-CONSENT LAW IS DERIVED HERE, AND THE TRANSLATION MOVES THE SAME WAY WITHOUT CITING IT. From 'we will call the girl and ask her' the chain derives that one may marry off an orphan only WITH HER CONSENT - a standing procedural rule taken from a narrative aside. Onkelos, independently, smooths the idiom 'ask her mouth' to 'HEAR WHAT SHE SAYS'. Both members of the declared reading make the verse about her answer; neither cites the other.

check.note: A consent requirement derived from a narrative question, converged on by the translation from the other direction.

middah: plain (ask-her read as the orphan's consent rule; Onkelos converging)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:12
claim_en: THE ANSWER IS READ AS DEFIANCE, NOT ASSENT. The doubled question is parsed as a hint - will you go, will you REALLY go - and her single word is read against her family rather than with it: I will go, against your will and without your approval. The chain reads a consent scene as a scene of consent overriding the household that staged it.

check.note: A one-word reply read as opposition to the questioners rather than agreement with them.

middah: plain (the answer read as defiance; the question's doubling, E10, inside)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:13
claim_en: THIS BLESSING IS READ AS INSINCERE, AND ITS FAILURE IS THE REASON A LATER PRAYER IS NEEDED. R. Aivu holds they blessed only with the mouth, downcast and despondent. The chain then draws the consequence forward: the conception waited for Isaac's own entreaty so that the idolaters could not say THEIR prayer bore fruit. The opening operator of gen_43 at 25:21 is therefore decided here, in a verse three chapters earlier and in a different block.

check.note: An evaluative reading of a blessing that supplies the causal reason for a later block's opening event.

middah: plain (a teacher's statement — an identification, a narrative expansion, a recorded dispute, or the verse's own wording read as the rule; no catalogued inference form)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:13; Onkelos Genesis 24:60
claim_en: THE BLESSING'S NUMBERS ARE SPLIT DEMOGRAPHICALLY, AND THE TRANSLATION DECLINES THE SPLIT. The chain reads thousands and myriads as two lines - chieftains from Esau, myriads from Jacob - with a dissent that both come from Israel. Onkelos joins the pair with an AND rather than dividing it, and separately expands the inherited GATE of the foes into their CITIES, territorializing the blessing. The two members read the same clause with opposite instincts: one divides, one joins.

check.note: A numeric pair divided by the midrash and joined by the translation, with an internal dissent recorded.

middah: plain (a teacher's statement — an identification, a narrative expansion, a recorded dispute, or the verse's own wording read as the rule; no catalogued inference form)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 68:9; Onkelos Genesis 24:63
claim_en: THE AFTERNOON PRAYER IS INSTITUTED AT THIS VERSE, BY BOTH MEMBERS AT ONCE. Isaac going out to meditate in the field toward evening is read as prayer, and the institution is seated here - the second of three, with the morning at 19:27 in gen_35 and the evening at 28:11 still ahead. Onkelos does not merely permit the reading: it WRITES it, rendering the verb TO PRAY. The same convergence pattern the machine already carries at 19:27, repeated - the chain stating the institution, the translation encoding it, neither citing the other. The correspondence with the daily offerings is recorded as the dissenting account.

check.note: A standing institution seated on one verse by the midrash and written into the same verse by the translation independently.

middah: I2 (to-meditate is prayer by the shared word — the afternoon prayer; Berakhot 26b; Onkelos writing it beside)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:15; Onkelos Genesis 24:64
claim_en: ONE VERB SOFTENED TWICE, BY TWO DIFFERENT DEVICES. The verse says she FELL from the camel. The chain softens it to INCLINED, proved from a verse about the one who stumbles but does not fall; Onkelos renders INCLINED HERSELF directly. Same destination, two routes - a proof-text on one side, a lexical choice on the other, and no citation between them.

check.note: An identical softening of one verb reached by proof-text and by translation independently.

middah: plain (fell softened to inclined by a proof-text; Onkelos's lexical choice beside)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:15
claim_en: THE DOCTRINE THAT THE TORAH'S GENERALITIES EXCEED ITS DETAILS IS MEASURED ON THIS VERSE. R. Eliezer takes 'all the matters that he had done' as proof that what the Torah states in general outweighs what it spells out - two or three further columns withheld behind one summarizing clause - against the Rabbis, who hold he related the praiseworthy matters. This is the second seat of the ink-economy meta-rule whose first seat the machine records at gen_40, and the pair brackets the repetition block from both ends.

check.note: A meta-rule about the text's own economy measured on a summarizing clause, disputed, and paired with an earlier seat.

middah: plain (the generalities-exceed-details meta-rule measured on all-the-matters)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:16; Onkelos Genesis 24:67
claim_en: THE TENT IS AN INSTRUMENTED ENVIRONMENT WHOSE SIGNATURE STATE RETURNS. Four conditions are recorded for the tent through Sarah's lifetime - a cloud at the entrance, the doors open wide, blessing in the dough, and a lamp burning from one Sabbath eve to the next - each of which CEASED at her death and RETURNED when Rebecca entered. And Onkelos absorbs the accompanying deeds-test into the verse itself: where the received ink has a ragged apposition, the translation writes that Isaac brought her in AND SAW, AND BEHOLD, HER DEEDS WERE PROPER LIKE THE DEEDS OF SARAH HIS MOTHER - a seeing-event and a judgment planted inside the verse. The largest translation delta of this sweep.

check.note: A place carrying four testable standing conditions across a succession, with the translation absorbing the midrash into the verse.

middah: plain (a teacher's statement — an identification, a narrative expansion, a recorded dispute, or the verse's own wording read as the rule; no catalogued inference form)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:16
claim_en: NARRATIVE ORDER IS READ AS A RULE OF PRECEDENCE. R. Yudan derives from the sequence - Isaac married at 24:67, then Abraham remarrying at 25:1 - that one marries off one's children before oneself. The claim is carried by the order of two verses across a block boundary and by nothing else, which makes the join between gen_41 and gen_42 load-bearing.

check.note: A precedence rule resting entirely on the order of two adjacent verses that straddle a block boundary.

middah: M-11 (Isaac's marriage before Abraham's remarriage — children first; the order across the block seam)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:14
claim_en: THE MOUNT IS READ AS A SIGN OF THE TWINS SHE HAS NOT YET BORNE. The camel carries one mark of purity and one of impurity, and the chain reads it as foreshadowing that she would produce one righteous and one wicked. R. Levi's plain answer - camels grow in the East - is recorded beside it rather than instead of it. The clause 'and she followed the man' is separately read as the walking-behind rule.

check.note: An animal's physical features read as a sign, with the naturalistic explanation preserved alongside.

middah: plain (a teacher's statement — an identification, a narrative expansion, a recorded dispute, or the verse's own wording read as the rule; no catalogued inference form)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:9
claim_en: A POLITE FORMULA IS CASHED AGAINST THE STANDING FAMILY MAP. 'I will turn to the right or to the left' is read as naming real alternatives rather than as a figure of speech - the right Ishmael, the left Lot - glossed by the identical idiom at 13:9, which the machine already carries at gen_29. What reads as deference becomes a threat with two named addresses.

check.note: An idiom read as naming specific persons, glossed by the same idiom's earlier occurrence in the corpus.

middah: E7 (right-or-left glossed by the identical idiom at 13:9)

source: Ketubot 57b:1-4; Yevamot 61b:12-14
claim_en: THE BRIDE'S YEAR. The family's days-or-ten clause read as the preparation-time law: 'days' is a YEAR by the redemption-days analogy (Lev 25:29), the two-days arm refused on speech-habit and the month arm on plain-from-plain derivation discipline — the virgin's twelve months (Rav Chisda). Beside it, 'virgin means only a maiden' seated definitionally on Rebekah's own 24:16. Filed F-119, auto-seated (round 32, the betrothal block).
middah: I2 (days is a year by the redemption-days analogy — the bride's year; Ketubot 57b)

source: Berakhot 61a:24
claim_en: RIDING BEHIND, NOT BEFORE. Rebekah's caravan went AFTER the man and not before him — the ordering as conduct law, the gradations recorded beside. Filed F-181, auto-seated (round 40, the conduct block).
middah: plain (after the man and not before him — the ordering as conduct; Berakhot 61a)
